definition: In machine learning, one-class classification (OCC), also known as unary classification or class-modelling, is an approach to the training of binary classifiers in which only examples of one of the two classes are used.
details: Examples include the monitoring of helicopter gearboxes, motor failure prediction, or assessing the operational status of a nuclear plant as 'normal': In such scenarios, there are few, if any, examples of the catastrophic system states – rare outliers – that comprise the second class. Alternatively, the class that is being focused on may cover a small, coherent subset of the data and the training may rely on an information bottleneck approach. In practice, counter-examples from the second class may be used in later rounds of training to further refine the algorithm.

explainer.lead: One-class classification, also called unary classification or class-modelling, trains a binary classifier using examples of only one of the two classes. It matters where examples of the second class are few or absent.

tiers.eli5: Like learning exactly what normal looks like so you can spot anything that isn't normal.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it for monitoring such as helicopter gearboxes, motor failure prediction, and nuclear plant status treated as 'normal', where catastrophic states are rare outliers. In practice, counter-examples from the second class can still be incorporated.
tiers.paperLevel: A binary classifier is trained with examples of only one class; the targeted class may instead cover a small, coherent subset of the data with training relying on an information bottleneck approach.

explainer.example: A nuclear plant model is trained only on 'normal' operational data, then flags deviations from that learned norm.
